chapter.name: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments

questions.q: Three housing societies of 450 flats in 9 blocks formed committees. P: all 450 owners sit together and no decision has been taken in three months. Q: the secretary picked 9 friends and three blocks have nobody to speak for them. R: each block elected one owner. Which conclusion agrees with the school story?
o: P fails as decisions cannot be reached, Q as many have no voice, and R avoids both
P is the most democratic because everyone sits on it, so its delay is no real fault at all
Q and R are equally democratic because both have 9 members on the committee
R is weak because nine owners could never know the needs of 450 flats
questions.a: The chapter finds that a committee of everyone cannot reach decisions or manage work, that a committee picked by one person leaves many without a role or voice, and that elected representatives from each group avoid both. Members' number does not decide whether a committee is democratic.

questions.q: In a small country, one council makes the rules, its own officers carry them out, and the same council punishes anyone who breaks them. Which statement fits the chapter's account of the three functions of government?
o: All three functions exist, even though one single body is the one that performs all of them
Only the executive function exists, as rule-making and punishing need separate bodies
The judicial function is missing, because the council that made the rules cannot punish
The country has to be a democracy, because all three functions are being performed
questions.a: The chapter says the legislative, executive and judicial functions can be performed by totally independent bodies or by the same body, so the three functions exist even when one body does them all. Having all three says nothing about democracy, and the same body can perform the judicial function.

questions.q: A Kolkata housing society's 900 residents all joined one committee and could not reach a single decision. Following the school story, each of its 9 blocks should now choose one ___ to sit on the committee.
questions.a: representative

questions.q:
Read the statements about government.
1. If one body makes the rules, carries them out and punishes those who break them, the judicial function no longer exists.
2. If the Head Teacher chooses the committee, most students have no role and no way to make their needs heard.
3. The first school method, in which everyone joins the committee, was set aside because decisions and implementation become hard to manage, not because anyone is left out.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the chapter says the three functions can be performed by independent bodies or by the same body. Statements 2 and 3 are the chapter's own reasoning on the second and first methods.

questions.q: True or False: A colony has 900 households in 30 lanes of 30 households each. A committee of 30 named by the colony secretary and a committee of 30 elected one per lane are equally democratic, because both have the same number of members. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. What makes a committee democratic is who chooses the members, not how many there are. Lane-elected members are chosen by the lanes they speak for; the secretary's picks leave most households with no role and no way to be heard.
s: Verdict False
Reason: who chooses, not the size

questions.q: Which of these descriptions wrongly pairs an action with a function of government?
o: A state assembly passes a rule that every school must have a library, which is the executive function as schools must obey it
The education department builds the libraries and appoints the staff under that rule, which is the executive function
A court examines a parent's complaint that one school was never given its library, which is the judicial function
Making the rule on libraries is the legislative function, a framework for running the state
questions.a: Passing a rule is the creation of rules, the legislative function. Obeying it is the work of others. Building libraries under the rule is executive and examining a complaint that the rule is ignored is judicial.

questions.q: In a Nagpur colony the secretary alone names the six residents of the welfare committee. The other 200 families have no way to tell the committee what they need. Which weakness from the school story does this match?
o: Like the Head Teacher choosing: most people have no real voice
Like everyone joining, the committee is too large to reach decisions
Like Grade 12 alone, only one group's problems would be known
Like voting, the chosen persons may fail to speak for their lanes
questions.a: A single person choosing the committee is the Head Teacher method: most people have no role and no way to be heard. A committee of six is not too large, and the options about one grade or about voting do not describe a nominated committee.

questions.q:
Match each committee in Column A with the result in Column B, as the school story reasons.
Column A: 1. All 3,000 villagers of a village sit on its committee.  2. The village head names five friends to the committee.  3. Each of the five lanes votes for one person to speak for it.  4. Only the oldest lane's elders form the committee.
Column B: a. Decisions and implementation become hard to manage  b. Many villagers have no role and no voice  c. Each lane has someone it believes will advocate its needs  d. The problems of the other lanes are not known to the committee
questions.a: Everyone joining makes decisions hard to manage; a nominated committee leaves most without a voice; election gives each lane an advocate; a committee from one group alone does not know the others' problems.

questions.q: Naghma proposed Grade 12 for the Student Committee and Shobha proposed Grade 11. (a) What flaw does Gurpreet's objection find in both proposals? (b) What extra flaw does Shobha's reply find in Naghma's proposal?
questions.a: (a) If only one grade runs everything, its students will not know the problems of the other grades. (b) Grade 12 will finish school in a few months, so it cannot go on doing the work.
s: Part (a): only one grade, so the problems of other grades are not known
Part (b): Grade 12 leaves school in a few months

questions.q: (a) A state starts a new road-building scheme, and its police patrol a crowded festival. Name the role of government from the chapter each one shows. (b) Officials set up kitchens in schools under a mid-day-meal law that the legislature has passed. Is setting up the kitchens a legislative, executive or judicial function? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The road scheme is delivering essential goods and services (infrastructure); the patrol is maintaining law and order. (b) Executive: the chapter calls implementing the rules and administering the country according to them the executive function, and the kitchens put an existing law into practice.
s: Both roles named correctly
Executive, with the reason that an existing law is being implemented

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the school story, a committee with one elected representative from each grade solves a problem that a committee of Grade 12 alone could not.
Reason (R): Students of Grade 12 alone would not know about the problems that other grades face.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: Gurpreet's objection is that one grade cannot know the problems of the others, which is exactly what representatives from every grade remove.

questions.q: A state's budget for the year is: roads Rs 40 crore, hospital equipment Rs 30 crore, police stations Rs 20 crore, talks with another country Rs 10 crore. What percentage of it goes to the role the chapter describes as delivering essential goods and services?
questions.a: Education, healthcare and infrastructure are the chapter's examples of essential goods and services, so roads and hospital equipment count: 40 + 30 = 70 of 100, which is 70%. Police stations are law and order and the talks are relations with other countries.

questions.q: A school has 12 sections of 40 students. Under the chapter's third method, how many students does the committee have and how many students does each member speak for? Why is this fairer than the Head Teacher picking 12 students who all come from Sections A and B?
questions.a: The committee has 12 members, one elected per section, and each speaks for 40 students (480 in all). If the 12 came from two sections, ten sections would have no role and no way to be heard.
s: 12 members, each speaking for 40 students
Picking from two sections leaves the other sections without a role or voice

questions.q: Tara says, 'The first and second school methods fail for the same reason: too many students are left out.' Do you agree? Use the school example.
questions.a: Partly right. The second method (Head Teacher chooses) does leave many students without a role or voice. The first method leaves nobody out; it fails because with everyone on the committee it is difficult to reach decisions and manage implementation.
s: Verdict: partly right
Second method: many students have no role or voice
First method: nobody is left out; it fails because decisions are hard to reach

questions.q: A state decides that every government school will have a library. Describe in three steps how the legislative, the executive and the judicial functions would each be involved.
questions.a: Legislative: the state's lawmakers pass the rule that schools get libraries. Executive: the education department builds libraries and appoints staff according to it. Judicial: if a school is denied its library, a court ensures the rule is followed.
s: Legislative function: creates the rule or law
Executive function: implements it and administers the work
Judicial function: ensures the rule is followed when it is not

questions.q: A region's government spends nothing on schools, hospitals or roads, but maintains an army and a police force. Using the chapter's list of roles, name the role it is neglecting and two roles it is performing.
questions.a: It neglects delivering essential goods and services (education, healthcare, infrastructure). It performs taking care of national defence (army) and maintaining law and order (police).
s: Neglected role: delivering essential goods and services
Performed roles: national defence and law and order

questions.q: Write a five-line story about a village committee for the street lights, in which the villagers choose their members in a democratic way. Show why all villagers do not sit on it.
questions.a: A good story has villagers voting for members from each lane (representation), a committee that acts for them on the lights, and a line saying a meeting of all villagers could not decide or manage the work smoothly.
s: Shows the villagers choosing representatives by voting
Shows the committee acting on the villagers' behalf on the task
Gives the reason why everyone cannot be on the committee: decisions and implementation become difficult

questions.q: 'The three functions of government are different jobs, but a country needs all three.' Justify with the help of a law on school meals, showing what could go wrong if any one function were missing.
questions.a: Legislative function: makes the rule on meals. Executive: carries it out through kitchens and staff. Judicial: ensures it is followed. Without the first there is no rule to follow; without the second the rule stays on paper; without the third nobody can make an ignoring school comply.
s: Defines the legislative, executive and judicial functions correctly
Applies each to the school meals law
Shows what goes wrong without the legislative or executive function
Shows what goes wrong without the judicial function

questions.q: A school has 1,260 students in 42 sections of 30 each. Evaluate the three options of the chapter for forming its Student Committee. Give the committee size under the first and third options, state the weakness of the second, and conclude which the school should use.
questions.a: The first method gives 1,260 members, so reaching decisions is difficult. The second method, the Head Teacher's choice, leaves most students without a voice. The third method gives 42 members, one chosen by each section who speaks for it. The school should use the third method, the democratic way.
s: First method: committee of 1,260 and the difficulty of deciding and implementing
Second method: most students have no role or voice
Third method: committee of 42, one chosen representative per section
Concludes in favour of electing representatives
Reason for the conclusion uses the other two weaknesses

questions.q:
The Student Sports Committee of a school in Pune has nine members, one elected by each of the nine sections of Class 7. It made a rule that every runner must register by 3 pm on Friday. The sports teacher's staff set up the registration desk and prepared the lane lists. Karan was refused a lane for registering at 3:20 pm, so he complained to the Head Teacher, who read the rule and the register. The Committee now suggests that it should also hear such complaints, to save time.
(a) Name the government function that each of these two actions resembles: making the rule, and setting up the registration desk.
(b) Which method of forming a committee from the chapter did the nine sections use, and why is it better than the sports teacher choosing nine friends?
(c) Which function is the Head Teacher performing in Karan's case, and why must it stay separate from the body that made the rule?
(d) Should the Committee hear complaints about its own rule? Give one gain and one risk and decide.
questions.a: (a) Legislative (making the rule) and executive (setting up the desk). (b) Election of representatives by voting; each section has a voice, unlike the nominated friends. (c) Judicial; if the Committee judged complaints about its own rule it would be the same body would be both rule-maker and the one deciding if the rule was broken, so a complaint may not be heard fairly. (d) Gain: quicker; risk: the body judges its own rule. A sensible decision keeps judging with an independent person such as the Head Teacher.
s: Part (a): legislative for making the rule, executive for setting up the desk
Part (b): election of representatives, each section gets a voice
Part (c): judicial, and why it must stay separate from the rule-maker
Part (d): one gain, one risk and a decision supported by them

questions.q:
Rampura village has 3,000 adults. To decide on repairing the village road, the head called all of them to the ground. About 1,100 came, argued until night and nothing was decided. A month later each of the 12 wards chose one member by voting. The 12 members met for two hours, decided on the repair and also passed a rule that no vehicle heavier than 5 tonnes may use the road.
(a) Which of the chapter's three school methods was tried first, and what went wrong with it?
(b) Which method did the village then use to form the group of 12?
(c) Which government function does the passing of the 5-tonne rule resemble?
(d) A villager says, 'Twelve people cannot speak for 3,000, so the whole village should decide everything.' Decide whether Rampura should go back, giving one cost and one benefit.
questions.a: (a) Everyone joins; decisions and implementation became difficult. (b) Election of representatives by voting. (c) Making a rule is the legislative function. (d) Keep representatives: a meeting of all gave no decision, while members chosen by voting decided in two hours. The cost is that a villager's voice is only through the member; the answer should weigh speed against being heard.
s: Part (a): the first method, everyone joins; decision-making stalled
Part (b): election of representatives by voting
Part (c): making a rule is the legislative function
Part (d): a decision with one cost and one benefit using parts (a) and (b)

questions.q: A law lets every adult vote but sends people to jail for criticising the government. Universal adult franchise is met, but the principle of ___ is not.
questions.a: freedom

questions.q: In Country P a written constitution says which body makes laws, which carries them out and which judges. In Country R the queen alone decides which body will make the laws and which will judge. (a) Which of the chapter's four key differences does this contrast show? (b) How does the chapter say this is decided in most democracies and in monarchies?
questions.a: (a) What the different parts of the government are and what they do. (b) In most democracies the system is written in a constitution, the book of fundamental rules; in monarchies it can be decided by the king or queen.
s: Key difference named: the parts of the government and what they do
Both ways of deciding stated: constitution in most democracies, king or queen in monarchies

questions.q: Four countries describe themselves. P: 'The head of a religious institution gives our government its authority.' Q: 'Our government is formed by an election every five years.' R: 'Our constitution says which body makes the laws and which judges.' S: 'Someone from the ruling king's family has always set up our government.' Which two statements answer the same one of the chapter's four key questions?
o: Q and S, because both of them say how the government comes to be formed
P and Q, because both say who gives the government its authority
R and S, because both say what the government is working for
P and R, because both say what the parts of the government do
questions.a: Q and S both tell how the government is formed (election in one, family continuing to rule in the other). P tells who gives the government authority, and R tells the parts of the government and what they do.

questions.q: True or False: In a district every citizen is equal before the law, so the district fully respects the chapter's idea of equality even if government hospitals take only the members of the ruling party's families. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says equality means equal treatment, equal access to facilities like education and health, and being equal before the law. Equality before the law alone does not cover hospitals reserved for a few families.
s: Verdict False
Reason: equality also means equal access to health and education

questions.q: A student matches practices to principles. Which match is WRONG?
o: A court cancels an order barring a child from school: representative participation
Every adult above 18 may vote in the ward election: universal adult franchise
Residents elect their ward member: representative participation
School and clinic open on equal terms to every child: equality
questions.a: A court protecting a family's rights shows an independent judiciary protecting fundamental rights, not representative participation (people electing representatives). The other three matches are right.

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Universal adult franchise means everyone in the country may vote.' Do you agree? Use the chapter's wording.
questions.a: Partly right. Universal adult franchise gives every citizen the right to vote, which is why it is called universal. But the chapter says it applies to citizens above a certain age, not to everyone, and the right is to choose a representative.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right: every citizen, whatever status, may vote
Wrong: it is for citizens above a certain age and to choose a representative

questions.q: (a) A court orders a state department to obey a law it had been ignoring. Which principle of democracy is at work? (b) Why would the order mean little if the department controlled the court?
questions.a: (a) Independent judiciary. (b) The judiciary must see that laws are followed by citizens and by all parts of the government; if the department controlled it, the part being checked would also be the judge, so the law could not be enforced on it.
s: Principle named
Why independence matters

questions.q:
Read the statements about democratic principles.
1. Equality in a democracy includes equal access to facilities like education and health, not only equality before the law.
2. Once a country gives every adult the vote, the chapter counts all its principles as put into practice.
3. In every government the system to decide how it will work is written in a constitution.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
questions.a: Statement 1 is the chapter's account of equality. Statement 2 is false: the principles are ideals and not all democracies put them in practice. Statement 3 is false: in monarchies it can be decided by the king or queen.

questions.q: A 12-year-old is paid nothing to work in a workshop. The owner says, 'She chose to work, and in a democracy citizens may make their own choices.' Which response agrees with the chapter?
o: Her right against exploitation is broken, since freedom lasts only until it harms another's rights
The owner is right, since freedom means she may choose work and nobody else is harmed
Nothing is broken, because equality only requires that all children in the workshop are treated alike
Nothing is broken, because only adults who can vote hold fundamental rights
questions.a: The chapter lists the right against exploitation among the fundamental rights a democracy protects, and says people may live as they like only until and unless it harms someone else's rights.

questions.q: The chapter gives 1928 for effective universal adult suffrage in the UK, 1950 for India and 1965 for the USA. (a) Put the three in order, earliest first. (b) How many years separate the UK and the USA, and what does it show about democracies?
questions.a: (a) UK (1928), India (1950), USA (1965). (b) 1965 - 1928 = 37 years; democracies differ in when they put the principles into practice, so they have evolved over time.
s: Correct order UK, India, USA
37 years, showing democracies differ in when principles were achieved

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Universal adult franchise was not present from the start in every democracy.
Reason (R): The UK and the USA both reached effective universal adult suffrage in the same year.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: India gave it in 1950, Swiss women only in 1971. R is false: the chapter gives 1928 for the UK and 1965 for the USA.

questions.q: Country T has 10 crore adults, but only the 6 crore who pay income tax may vote. Which conclusion fits the chapter?
o: 4 crore adults are shut out, so universal adult franchise is incomplete in T
6 crore adults are shut out, so universal adult franchise is incomplete in T
4 crore adults are shut out, so T lacks an independent judiciary
No adult is shut out, because every taxpayer is a citizen and citizens may vote
questions.a: 10 - 6 = 4 crore adults, 40 percent, cannot vote. Universal adult franchise gives every citizen above a certain age the vote, so it is incomplete. Voting rights do not show whether the judiciary is independent.

questions.q: A country has this law: 'Only men above 25 may vote, and anyone who criticises the ruler in public is punished.' Show that this country cannot be called one that follows the chapter's principles, naming the principles broken.
questions.a: It breaks universal adult franchise, since women and younger adults are not allowed to vote; it breaks freedom, since citizens cannot express their opinions; it also breaks equality, since people are not treated equally.
s: Universal adult franchise broken: only some adults may vote
Freedom broken: opinions cannot be expressed
Equality broken: not all people are treated alike, so the law cannot follow the principles

questions.q: A citizen wants to find out which kind of goal her government is designed for: equality and prosperity for all, or prosperity of some families only. (a) Under which of the chapter's key questions does this fall? (b) Give one thing she can check about hospitals and schools that the principle of equality would require.
questions.a: (a) What the government is working for, its goals. (b) Whether everyone has equal access to facilities like education and health, regardless of the family they belong to.
s: Key question named: what is the government working for
Check: equal access to education and health for all

questions.q: Dev compares India with Country Z on the four key questions. Z's answers: its authority comes from its people; the government is formed by elections; a written constitution sets out its parts; it is designed to raise the prosperity of two ruling families. On which question do India and Z differ?
o: Only on the question of what the government is working for, its goal
On who decides that this is the government, and on how it is formed
On the parts of the government and what they do, since only India has a constitution
On every one of the four questions, since Z is not a democracy
questions.a: Z answers the first three questions as India does. It differs only in the goal: India works towards equality and prosperity for all, Z for two families.

questions.q: Tara says, 'If a country holds elections, it automatically follows all the principles of democracy described on pages 191-192.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. Elections show representative participation, but the chapter lists five more principles, and says not all democracies are able to put them in practice. For example the UK reached effective universal adult suffrage only in 1928 and the USA by 1965, long after they adopted democracy.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Names elections as only one principle, representative participation, among the others (equality, freedom, universal adult franchise, fundamental rights, independent judiciary)
Supports with the chapter's statement that principles are ideals, with the UK or USA suffrage dates

questions.q: Ria notes that Indian women could vote from 1950 and Swiss women from 1971. For how many years did the Swiss women lack a vote that Indian women already had, and what does it show?
o: 21 years, which shows that democratic principles have evolved and differ between democracies
21 years, which shows that Switzerland was not a democracy before 1971
29 years, which shows that democratic principles have evolved and differ between democracies
20 years, which shows that India is the older democracy of the two
questions.a: 1971 - 1950 = 21 years. The chapter uses these two dates to show that even fundamental principles evolved over time; the table gives 1848 as the year Switzerland established democracy, so it was a democracy earlier.

questions.q: Compare a democracy such as India with a kingdom on three of the chapter's key questions: how the government is formed, what the parts of the government are and what they do, and what it is working for. Then analyse which of the three shows the widest gap.
questions.a: Formation: democracy through elections; kingdom, someone from within the family continues. Parts: constitution written in a book in most democracies, whereas the king or queen may decide in monarchy; the three functions may be performed by independent bodies or by the same body. Goals: India works for equality and prosperity for all, while some governments are designed for the prosperity of some families. The widest gap is argued, for example the goals.
s: Formation compared
Parts and functions compared, with constitution against the monarch
Goals compared: all against some families
Chooses one as the widest gap
Gives a reason for the choice

questions.q: Sundarpur's Ward 9 in Nashik is about to elect its ward member. Show how four of these principles would look in this election: equality, freedom, representative participation and universal adult franchise. Then say why a ward may still fall short of some of them.
questions.a: Equality: every person is treated equally and is equal before the law. Freedom: people express opinions on candidates freely. Representative participation: residents elect the member, who then acts for the ward. Universal adult franchise: every adult resident has one vote regardless of sex, wealth or status. Principles are ideals, which are not always fully put into practice.
s: Equality applied to the election
Freedom applied to the election
Representative participation applied: the ward elects the member
Universal adult franchise applied: every adult gets a vote
Explains that the principles are ideals not always practised

questions.q:
Two schools in Jaipur are compared. In Trust School, the founding family's trust decides the rules and the timetable, names the prefects and spends the school fund on its own guest house. In Open School, students vote for one representative per class, all grades use the library equally, and any student may write opinions in the school magazine. Trust School's results are better and its decisions are quick.
(a) For each school, say who decides and what the school is working for.
(b) Name two democratic principles visible in Open School and where each appears.
(c) Which of the chapter's four key differences between governments does the spending of the school fund illustrate?
(d) A parent must choose a school. Using the chapter, give your decision and one point on each side.
questions.a: (a) Trust School: the trust decides, and works for the trust's interests; Open School: students share the decision, working for all students. (b) Representative participation: the voting for representatives; freedom: writing opinions in the magazine; equality: equal use of the library. (c) What the government is working for. (d) A decision with a point on each side, for example Open School for democratic principles despite slower decisions.
s: Part (a): the trust against the students as deciders, with the aims
Part (b): two principles named with where each appears
Part (c): what the government is working for
Part (d): a decision with a point for each school

questions.q:
Dhara is a country with 8 crore adults, of whom 4 crore are men. From its first election in 1952 only men could vote; women were given the vote in 1974. Its leaders say, 'We were a democracy from 1952, because we hold elections and have courts.'
(a) Which fundamental principle of democracy was incomplete in Dhara until 1974?
(b) What does the chapter's example of Switzerland add to Dhara's story?
(c) Are the leaders right as it stands, or only partly right? Give reasons.
(d) What percentage of Dhara's adults could vote in 1952, and what does it show about the leaders' claim?
questions.a: (a) Universal adult franchise. (b) Switzerland's women voted only from 1971: principles are ideals that democracies reach over time. (c) Partly right: elections and courts are features, but the principle of universal adult franchise was not met. (d) 4/8 = 50%; half the adults were left out, so the claim is only partly true.
s: Part (a): universal adult franchise
Part (b): the Swiss example linked, principles are ideals reached over time
Part (c): a reasoned partly-right verdict
Part (d): 50 percent, tied to the claim

questions.q:
Greenfield School in Nagpur has 1,200 students in 20 equal classes. It is choosing between two designs for its student council. Design P: each class elects one representative; the 20 representatives then select a leader and team from among themselves, who continue only while most representatives trust them. Design Q: all 1,200 students vote directly for a Council President for one year; the President picks a team that does not sit in, or depend on, any student body.
(a) Which design follows the pattern of a parliamentary democracy, and which a presidential one?
(b) In which design can the team be removed during the year by the representatives losing confidence?
(c) How many students does each representative speak for in Design P?
(d) The school must choose one design. Give your choice with one gain and one risk of it.
questions.a: (a) P is parliamentary, Q is presidential. (b) In Design P. (c) 1200/20 = 60 students. (d) For example P: team stays accountable to the representatives, but changes of team can be frequent; Q: the leader is directly chosen by everyone for a fixed year, but is not answerable to any body in between.
s: Part (a): P parliamentary, Q presidential
Part (b): Design P, because the team continues only with confidence
Part (c): 60 students
Part (d): a choice with one gain and one risk

questions.q: Which situation is possible in a parliamentary democracy but NOT in a presidential democracy as the chapter describes them?
o: A minister who sits in the legislature as one of its members
A head of the executive chosen directly by the voters
A judiciary independent of the executive and legislature
General elections held at regular and fixed intervals
questions.a: In a parliamentary democracy the members of the executive are also part of the legislature. In a presidential democracy the executive works independently of it. Direct election of the head, an independent judiciary and fixed-interval elections are not features exclusive to the parliamentary form.

questions.q: Country A holds general elections every five years, like India, and Country B every four years, like the USA. Both held one in 2020. (a) Give the next two election years of each. (b) What reason does the chapter give for holding elections at regular and fixed intervals?
questions.a: (a) A: 2025 and 2030; B: 2024 and 2028. (b) So that people can express changes in their choices through elections.
s: Four correct years
Reason for fixed intervals

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a presidential democracy the head of the executive can stay in office even when the legislature opposes him.
Reason (R): In a presidential democracy the head of the executive is elected by the people and does not need the legislature's confidence.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both true and R explains A: because the president's position does not depend on the legislature's confidence, opposition in the legislature cannot end it.

questions.q: Country Y's head of the executive is directly elected by the people, is also a member of the legislature, and must resign when the legislature withdraws confidence. Show that Y cannot match either the parliamentary or the presidential form exactly as the chapter describes them.
questions.a: Direct election of the head is a presidential feature, but sitting in the legislature and needing its confidence are parliamentary features. The chapter makes the two forms opposite on this point: in a parliamentary form the executive is part of the legislature and needs its confidence; in a presidential form it works independently and does not need it. Y mixes both, so it fits neither completely.
s: Names the presidential feature: directly elected head
Names the parliamentary features: inside the legislature and needs confidence
Concludes that the forms are opposite on this point so Y matches neither fully

questions.q: In Country N the head of the executive stays in office even after the legislature declares that it has no confidence in him. By the chapter's description, N is not a ___ democracy.
questions.a: parliamentary

questions.q: In Country K, the minister who runs the police names the judges and can dismiss them. (a) Does K have separation of power as the chapter explains it? (b) What is the danger to the judicial function?
questions.a: (a) No: the judiciary is not independent of the executive, whereas separation of power means the three organs work independently and do not interfere in each other's functions. (b) Judges would depend on the minister, so they cannot freely ensure that the rules are followed by the executive itself.
s: Verdict No with the meaning of separation of power
Danger to the judicial function

questions.q: Table 9.1 gives these rows. India: prime minister and council of ministers, Lok Sabha more powerful than Rajya Sabha. USA: president, Senate and House of Representatives of equal power. South Korea: president, a single house. Australia: prime minister and council of ministers, two houses of equal power. Which pair has two houses of equal power but different kinds of executive?
o: Australia and the USA
India and Australia
The USA and South Korea
India and South Korea
questions.a: Australia and the USA both have two houses of equal power, but Australia has a prime minister with a council of ministers and the USA a president. India and Australia share the executive; the USA and South Korea share the president; India and South Korea differ in both.

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the term in Column B.
Column A: 1. All 300 adults of a hamlet meet and decide each matter together.  2. Voters choose MPs, and some MPs become ministers who stay only with the legislature's confidence.  3. Voters directly choose a head of the executive who does not need the legislature's confidence.  4. A government must explain its decisions to the people who elected it.
Column B: a. Presidential democracy  b. Accountability  c. Direct democracy  d. Parliamentary democracy
questions.a: A meeting of all adults is direct democracy; ministers drawn from the legislature who need its confidence are parliamentary; a directly elected head who needs no confidence is presidential; answering to the electors is accountability.

questions.q: True or False: In India the prime minister and council of ministers are members of Parliament, so in India the executive, the legislature and the judiciary are all completely independent of one another. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. In a parliamentary democracy the executive is part of the legislature. Table 9.1 shows only the judiciary as independent of the executive and the legislature.
s: Verdict False
Reason: the executive sits in the legislature

questions.q: A country has 12 crore voters and a legislature of 800 members. (i) How many voters does each member represent, if equal? (ii) Why would direct democracy be hard here? (iii) How can voters still hold the government accountable?
questions.a: (i) 12,00,00,000 / 800 = 1,50,000 voters per member. (ii) Everyone taking part in every decision would be very hard in a large country, as in the school story. (iii) Through elections held at fixed intervals.
s: (i) 1,50,000 voters per member
(ii) Direct decision-making by all is very hard in large countries
(iii) Elections at regular fixed intervals make the government answerable

questions.q: The government of Country M, a representative democracy, cancels the next general election for ten years, saying, 'The people already chose us.' Which feature of representative democracy does this damage most directly?
o: The chance to express changes in choices at regular, fixed intervals
The Lower House being more powerful than the Upper House in matters of law
The independence of the judiciary from the executive and the legislature
The practice of the executive sitting inside the legislature
questions.a: The chapter says elections at regular and fixed intervals let people express changes in their choices. The other options are about the relative power of the houses, the judiciary, or the parliamentary form, not about elections being held.

questions.q: (a) According to Table 9.1, name one feature India and Australia share and one in which they differ. (b) Name the form of democracy the chapter says India has, and say whether the people elect India's executive directly.
questions.a: (a) Shared: a prime minister and council of ministers as the executive (or an independent judiciary); different: the Lower House is more powerful in India while the two houses have equal power in Australia. (b) Parliamentary democracy; the people elect the legislature, not the executive, and ministers are selected from among its members.
s: One shared and one different feature
Parliamentary; people elect the legislature, not the executive

questions.q: Isha says, 'A president who does not need the legislature's confidence is still chosen by the people, so a presidential democracy is also accountable to the people.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. A presidential democracy is a form of representative democracy in which the president is elected by the people. In a representative democracy the government is always accountable to the people who elected it, and elections at regular fixed intervals let the people change their choice, even though the president does not need the legislature's confidence.
s: Verdict: yes
The president is elected by the people; presidential democracy is a representative democracy
Accountability through elections at fixed intervals, not through the legislature's confidence

questions.q: (a) From Table 9.1, which of these are Lower Houses: Lok Sabha, Senate, House of Representatives? (b) The chapter says the Lower House is 'generally more powerful'. Does that hold for India and the USA? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Lok Sabha and House of Representatives. (b) It holds for India, where the Lok Sabha is more powerful than the Rajya Sabha, but not for the USA, where the Senate and House of Representatives have equal power, which is why the chapter says 'generally'.
s: Lower Houses identified
India fits, USA is an exception

questions.q: A student says, 'South Korea and the USA have the same legislature, because each has a president.' Which correction agrees with Table 9.1?
o: The executives match, but South Korea has one house and the USA has two of equal power
The executives differ, because South Korea has a prime minister and the USA a president
The legislatures match, but South Korea's judiciary depends on the executive and the USA's does not
Nothing needs correcting, because a president always comes with the same two-house legislature
questions.a: The table shows a president in both, but a single house (National Assembly) in South Korea and a Senate and House of Representatives of equal power in the USA. Both judiciaries are shown as independent.

questions.q: A hall holds 5,000 people. A country has 12 crore voters who are to take every decision together, as in a direct democracy. (a) How many such hallfuls of people would there be? (b) What does the chapter say about carrying out direct democracy in larger countries?
questions.a: (a) 12,00,00,000 / 5,000 = 24,000 hallfuls, which shows that a single decision-making meeting is impractical. (b) The chapter says it is very hard to carry out, particularly in larger countries, as the school story showed when everyone joined the committee.
s: 24,000 hallfuls
Direct democracy is very hard to carry out in large countries

questions.q: A news report says: 'The Prime Minister's government fell after the Lok Sabha withdrew its support.' Which statement from the chapter best explains this event?
questions.a: In a parliamentary democracy the council of ministers is accountable to the legislature and works only with its confidence. The other statements are also true, but they explain a presidential office, the make-up of the houses, or the election interval, not the fall.
o: The council of ministers continues working only while it has the Lok Sabha's confidence
The president does not need the legislature's confidence to hold his or her position
The Lower House is elected by direct voting and is generally the more powerful house
General elections in India take place at regular and fixed intervals of five years

questions.q:
Read the statements about forms of democracy.
1. In a direct democracy, citizens elect representatives who take all the decisions for them.
2. In a parliamentary democracy, the people elect the legislature and the executive separately by direct vote.
3. In the USA, general elections occur every four years.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 3 is correct. Direct democracy has citizens decide directly, not through representatives; and in a parliamentary democracy the people elect the legislature but not the executive.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q: Compare presidential and parliamentary democracy on (a) how the executive is chosen, (b) whether the executive is part of the legislature, and (c) whether it needs the legislature's confidence. Use India and the USA, then analyse which gives the government more security in office.
questions.a: Parliamentary (India): the legislature is elected and ministers are selected from it; the executive is part of the legislature; the council of ministers needs the confidence of the Lok Sabha. Presidential (USA): the president is elected by the people; the executive works independently of the legislature; no confidence needed. So the presidential form gives more security in office.
s: Executive chosen: ministers from the elected legislature against the president elected by the people
Executive part of the legislature in a parliamentary and independent in a presidential democracy
Confidence of the legislature needed against not needed
Concludes that the presidential form gives more security in office
Reasons the conclusion from the confidence rule

questions.q: Country X holds elections every five years, but its government does not have to explain its decisions to anyone and ignores the voters between elections. Compare it with a representative democracy such as India, using five points from the chapter, and say whether elections alone make X a representative democracy.
questions.a: In India people elect representatives through universal adult franchise; the government is accountable to those who elected it; elections occur at regular fixed intervals; elections let people express changes in their choices; the people do not govern directly, so their power works through elections. X has elections but lacks accountability, so elections alone do not make it a representative democracy.
s: Representatives elected through universal adult franchise
Government accountable to those who elected it, which X lacks
Regular fixed intervals of elections
Elections let people express changes in choice
Concludes that elections without accountability do not make X a representative democracy

questions.q:
Two fictional countries are compared. In Alfa, the ministers are members of the legislature and continue only while they have its confidence. In Beta, the president is elected directly by the people, works independently of the legislature and does not need its confidence.
(a) Which of the two follows the parliamentary pattern and which the presidential, as the chapter describes them?
(b) If Alfa's legislature withdraws confidence in its ministers, what does the chapter's rule say about their working?
(c) A citizen wants a poorly performing government to end before the next general election. Which system suits her, and what does she give up?
(d) Beta's citizens propose that the legislature, not the people, should choose the president. Give one gain and one loss and decide.
questions.a: (a) Alfa parliamentary, Beta presidential. (b) The ministers cannot continue working, since they work only while they have the legislature's confidence. (c) Alfa suits her, because ministers can lose office when confidence goes; she gives up the direct vote for the head of the executive and the independence from the legislature. (d) Gain: the head would answer to the legislature between elections. Loss: the people would no longer elect the head directly. Any decision that uses the gain and the loss is accepted.
s: Part (a): Alfa parliamentary, Beta presidential
Part (b): the ministers cannot continue without the legislature's confidence
Part (c): Alfa chosen, with what she gives up
Part (d): a gain, a loss and a decision using them

questions.q: True or False: In many parts of ancient India a raja could inherit his throne and still not have power that was absolute or beyond question. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the power of the raja was neither absolute nor beyond question in many parts of India: he was expected to decide within the limits of rajadharma and was guided by bodies such as the sabha or samiti.
s: Verdict True
Reason: rajadharma and sabha or samiti limited him

questions.q: Which piece of evidence in the chapter tells us about rules on WHO could take part in a body, and not just that a body met?
o: The Uttaramerur inscriptions, which record the qualifications and duties of members
The Vajji account, which says that representatives from various clans met regularly
Kalhana's story, in which the king asks the cobbler's permission before removing the hut
Bhishma's teaching, which says that the welfare of the people is the raja's highest priority
questions.a: The Uttaramerur inscriptions give the election process, the qualifications of members, their duties and the conditions for dismissal, so they show rules about who could take part. The others describe meetings, a king's conduct or advice.

questions.q: 'A republic is always more democratic than a monarchy.' Judge this using the Greek republics, the Vajji republic and the Uttaramerur inscriptions.
questions.a: Greek republics: in some regions only free men voted and women, workers and slaves did not; elsewhere only a small privileged group decided. Vajji: an early republic with leaders chosen on merit, elections for key positions and representatives of clans meeting regularly. Uttaramerur: under a king, yet members of the village sabha were elected with sealed ballot boxes and removed for corruption. The label alone does not decide how democratic a government is; who takes part and how leaders are chosen do, so the claim is false.
s: Greek republics with limited voting
Vajji's merit, elections and regular meetings
Uttaramerur: elections to the sabha under a king
Concludes the claim is not always true
Reason: who takes part and how leaders are chosen matter more than the label

questions.q: A country's head of state is elected for a term and does not belong to any royal family. (a) Is it a republic by the chapter's definition? Why? (b) Name the early Indian example given in the chapter and one way its leaders were chosen.
questions.a: (a) Yes: a republic is a government whose head of state is elected and is not a hereditary monarch. (b) The Vajji mahajanapada (Lichchhavi clan); leaders were chosen on merit rather than birth, and key positions were filled through elections.
s: Republic with the definition applied
Vajji with one way leaders were chosen

questions.q:
Read the statements about early republics and kingship.
1. The Uttaramerur inscriptions show that a village body in the Chola period chose its members by election.
2. Because Greece and Rome had republics in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, every adult living there could vote.
3. A republic differs from a monarchy in that its head of state is elected, whereas a monarch inherits the position.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statement 1 is from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: in some regions of Greece free men could vote but women, workers and slaves could not, and elsewhere only a small privileged group decided. Statement 3 follows the chapter's definition of a republic and its account of monarchs.

questions.q: A quiz says, 'Before modern times people never had a say in who took decisions for them.' Anu cites the Vajji mahajanapada and Ben cites the Uttaramerur inscriptions. Which statement about their evidence is correct?
o: Both contradict it: Vajji was an early republic, and Uttaramerur had village elections under a king
Only Anu's evidence holds, because the Uttaramerur sabha was not chosen by any kind of election
Only Ben's evidence holds, because the leaders of Vajji were chosen by birth and not by merit
Neither holds, because the chapter places both in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE
questions.a: Vajji's leaders were chosen on merit with elections for key positions, and the clan representatives met regularly, so it is called an early republic. Uttaramerur, in the Chola period (10th century CE), had sealed-ballot elections to the village sabha even though a king held power.

questions.q: Compare the Uttaramerur inscriptions and Kalhana's story. (a) What does the inscription show that checked members of the village sabha? (b) What checked the king's conduct in the story, and how is that different in kind from (a)?
questions.a: (a) Members who were corrupt were removed immediately, under rules written in the inscriptions. (b) The king's own commitment to dharma checked him: he asked the cobbler's permission and paid compensation. The first is a written rule applied to members; the second is the ruler's own restraint.
s: (a) Written rule of immediate removal for corruption
(b) The king's own commitment to dharma, a restraint of the ruler rather than a rule applied to members

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Chandrapida's treatment of the cobbler shows a king acting within the limits of rajadharma.
Reason (R): Chandrapida had the cobbler's hut removed by force, because a temple to his deity mattered more than a lowly subject's home.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: he asked the cobbler's permission respectfully and paid adequate compensation. R is false: the king did not use force; he asked, and the cobbler agreed.

questions.q: Kabir says, 'The Uttaramerur village elections took place under the Chola kings, so the kings themselves must have been elected.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The inscriptions describe the election of members of the village sabha, a local administrative body. The chapter says such voices were valued even when power was in the hands of a king or queen, which means the king was a separate ruler; monarchs inherit the position, whereas the head of state of a republic is elected.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The election was for the village sabha, not for the king
The chapter says people's voice counted even when power was with a king; a monarch is not elected

questions.q: Which of these royal decisions goes against ALL the points that Bhishma taught Yudhishthira?
o: A king dismisses his advisors, saying they only create doubts, and decides alone as his own right
A king listens to a farmer's complaint about his flooded field and pays him fair compensation
A king reminds his whole court that his authority is only temporary and bound by dharma
A king consults several wise advisors before a decision that will affect the whole kingdom
questions.a: Bhishma says a raja must seek guidance from wise advisors, must not be attached to power, and that his authority is temporary and bound by dharma; deciding alone with the advisors removed rejects those teachings. The other three decisions follow his teachings.

questions.q: Compare a king who follows rajadharma with one who believes he has divine powers. Apply both to the cobbler's hut in Kalhana's story and analyse who is more likely to treat the cobbler fairly.
questions.a: A king under rajadharma rules according to dharma for the welfare of all and applies the law without bias, as Chandrapida did by asking the cobbler's permission and paying compensation. A king who thinks he is divine may feel no need to listen or to ask, and might simply order the hut removed. The first is more likely to treat the cobbler fairly because he accepts that his authority is bound by dharma.
s: Defines the king under rajadharma
Describes a king claiming divine powers
Applies rajadharma to the cobbler: permission and compensation
Applies the divine-claim king to the cobbler: forced removal
Concludes with a reason about fairness

questions.q: In a kingdom the king may not levy any new tax until the sabha agrees, and he cannot overrule it. By the chapter's wording, the king's power in that kingdom is not ___.
questions.a: absolute

questions.q: Compare the early republic of Vajji with the areas of Greece where only a small, privileged group made the decisions. (a) Who took part in decisions in each? (b) Which would you call the wider-based, and why?
questions.a: (a) In Vajji, representatives from various clans met regularly and leaders were chosen on merit; in those parts of Greece, only a small privileged group decided. (b) Vajji is wider-based, since decisions involved representatives of several clans, not a small privileged group.
s: (a) Vajji: representatives of various clans; Greek areas: a small privileged group
(b) Vajji wider-based with the reason

questions.q: In Kalhana's story the king first blamed the builders for not asking the cobbler's permission, then received the cobbler and, after the hut was given up, paid him adequate money. Which inference is best supported by the passage?
o: Even a lowly subject's home was not to be taken without respectful permission and compensation
The king gave up the idea of the temple altogether because the cobbler refused to move
The cobbler agreed to leave only because a sabha ordered the king to compensate him
The king paid the compensation only to stop the builders from complaining about him again
questions.a: The cobbler said he would let go of the hut if the king respectfully asked, and the king did so and gave adequate compensation; the cobbler praised the king's commitment to dharma even towards a lowly subject. The story does not mention a sabha or the temple being given up.

questions.q: A village of 6 wards will set up a sabha of 6 members, modelled on the Uttaramerur inscriptions. Write three rules for it, and for each rule say which detail of the inscriptions it follows.
questions.a: For example: each ward chooses one member by placing its choice in a sealed ballot box (sealed ballot boxes); a member must meet stated qualifications and carry out stated duties (qualifications and duties); a member found guilty of corruption is removed at once (conditions for dismissal).
s: A rule on the election by ward, tied to sealed ballot boxes
A rule on qualifications and duties, tied to the inscriptions
A rule on immediate removal for corruption, tied to the inscriptions

questions.q: Kalhana's story ends, 'For those who desire happiness, there should be no false pride.' Which of Bhishma's teachings does this echo most closely?
o: A raja must not get attached to power, which fosters ego
A raja must seek guidance from wise advisors for informed decisions
A raja must apply the law without bias, to ensure fairness
A raja must make the welfare of his people his highest priority
questions.a: No false pride matches Bhishma's warning that attachment to power fosters ego and corruption. The other teachings are real but concern advisors, fairness and the people's welfare, which other parts of the story show.

questions.q: Bhishma says a raja's authority is 'temporary and bound by dharma'. (a) Explain in one sentence how this limits a raja. (b) Show the limit at work in Kalhana's story.
questions.a: (a) A raja cannot rule as he pleases; he must stay within dharma and look to the welfare of all, because his authority is temporary. (b) Chandrapida did not remove the cobbler's hut by force; he asked permission and paid adequate compensation.
s: (a) Rule within dharma for the welfare of all, not as he pleases
(b) Asking permission and paying compensation instead of forcing the cobbler

questions.q: Chandrapida's behaviour towards the cobbler shows two of Bhishma's points. Name the two points and give the part of Kalhana's passage that shows each.
questions.a: Welfare of his people comes first, shown by the adequate compensation he paid the cobbler. Not getting attached to power or ego, shown by Kalhana's line 'For those who desire happiness, there should be no false pride', and by the king asking the cobbler's permission instead of forcing him.
s: First point: welfare of the people, with the compensation as evidence
Second point: not attached to power or ego, with the 'no false pride' line or the request for permission
Links the story to the idea that the raja's authority is bound by dharma

questions.q:
A village sabha in a Chola-style kingdom has 8 members. Members are chosen from the village's wards by putting choices in a sealed ballot box, and a member found guilty of corruption is removed at once. In six years, 3 of the 8 members were found guilty and replaced. A villager now proposes that any member who is late to a meeting should also be removed at once. An elder replies that the inscriptions named particular conditions for dismissal and that corruption is the one that calls for immediate removal.
(a) What percentage of the sabha's members were removed in the six years?
(b) Does the removal of three members show that the dismissal rule worked? Give a reason using the chapter.
(c) Name two features of the Uttaramerur inscriptions that this sabha follows.
(d) Should the villager's proposal be accepted? Give one gain, one risk and your decision.
questions.a: (a) 3/8 = 37.5 percent. (b) Yes, the rule worked: members who were corrupt were removed at once, as the inscriptions say; it does not by itself show the election failed. (c) Sealed ballot boxes and conditions leading to dismissal (corruption). (d) Gain: members would take their duties more seriously. Risk: the sabha could lose members for small faults and the conditions the inscriptions name would be ignored. Any decision that uses the gain and the risk is accepted.
s: Part (a): 37.5 percent
Part (b): the rule worked, since the corrupt were removed at once
Part (c): sealed ballot boxes and dismissal conditions
Part (d): a gain, a risk and a decision

questions.q:
A museum card describes a model town of ancient Greece in the 4th century BCE with 10,000 people: 3,000 free men, 3,500 women, 2,500 workers and 1,000 slaves. Only free men could vote. The card's title is undecided between 'A Republic', 'A Democracy like Today's India' and 'A Republic with Limited Voting'.
(a) How many people could vote, and what percentage of the town was that?
(b) Which groups could not vote, according to the chapter?
(c) Which principle of today's democracies, mentioned in the chapter, was missing?
(d) Which title tells visitors the most, and why? Justify with the chapter's definition of a republic.
questions.a: (a) 3,000 people; 3000/10000 = 30%. (b) Women, workers and slaves. (c) Universal adult franchise (equality is also accepted). (d) 'A Republic with Limited Voting' tells the most: Greece's regions were called republics by the chapter, but not everyone could vote, so it was not like today's India with universal adult franchise.
s: Part (a): 3,000 people, 30 percent
Part (b): women, workers and slaves
Part (c): universal adult franchise
Part (d): the third title, justified with the republic definition and the limited vote

questions.q: In Land L the monarch opens parliament each year, but the laws are passed by an elected parliament and a prime minister heads the executive. Seema says, 'L has a king, so the king rules.' Ravi says, 'L has a parliament, so L has stopped being a monarchy.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: Seema is wrong about who rules, but L is still a monarchy, with a king of nominal power
Seema is right, because in every monarchy the head of state holds the real executive power
Ravi is right, because a country with an elected parliament cannot also have a monarch as head
Both are right, because the king rules in ceremonies and the parliament rules at other times
questions.a: As in the UK, the head of state is a king or queen with only nominal power; the parliament makes the laws and the prime minister exercises executive power. This is called a constitutional monarchy.

questions.q: True or False: A country whose head of state inherits the throne can still, in practice, be governed as a parliamentary democracy. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The United Kingdom has a king or queen as head of state with only nominal power; the elected parliament makes the laws and the prime minister with the Council of Ministers exercises executive power, so it is a constitutional monarchy and in practice a parliamentary democracy.
s: Verdict True
Reason from the United Kingdom's example

questions.q:
Read the statements about monarchy and theocracy.
1. In a constitutional monarchy the monarch exercises the real executive power while the parliament only advises.
2. A country can be classed as a theocracy even though it has an elected president and parliament, as Iran shows.
3. In Saudi Arabia the council that advises the king can overrule him, since he governs according to Islamic law.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
questions.a: Statement 2 is the chapter's account of Iran. Statement 1 is false: in a constitutional monarchy the prime minister exercises the real executive power. Statement 3 is false: the king appoints the council and is not bound by its advice.

questions.q: A country keeps its king as head of state, but an elected parliament makes every law and a prime minister runs the executive. A visiting student who reads the chapter would say it is really a ___ democracy (one word).
questions.a: parliamentary

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Only an absolute monarch can have authority over making, enforcing and judging laws all together.' Show, using Iran, that this cannot be true.
questions.a: An absolute monarch such as the king of Saudi Arabia holds complete control of making laws, ensuring they are followed and adjudicating. But Iran's Supreme Leader, selected by clerics for life, has the ultimate authority over the legislature, executive and judiciary, and Iran is described as a theocracy and not a monarchy. So authority over all three can exist outside an absolute monarchy.
s: States what the absolute monarch controls
Shows the Supreme Leader's ultimate authority over all three organs
Concludes that Iran is not an absolute monarchy, so the claim fails

questions.q: Which single change would turn the United Kingdom, as the chapter describes it, into an absolute monarchy?
o: The king or queen takes over making laws, enforcing them and judging all disputes in the land
Parliament passes a larger number of laws in a year than it did in earlier years
A new prime minister takes over after a change in the elected parliament majority
The king or queen opens parliament in a ceremonial coach on one day every year
questions.a: An absolute monarch has complete control in making laws, ensuring that they are followed and adjudicating when they are not. The other changes leave the real power with the elected parliament and the prime minister.

questions.q: A queen dies and her son becomes the new king. (a) Which feature of monarchy does this show? (b) Does it tell us whether the new king will be an absolute or a constitutional monarch? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Monarchies are usually hereditary, and typically the eldest son of the ruling monarch becomes the next king. (b) No: inheritance only shows how the position passes on. What decides the type is who makes the laws and holds executive power, the monarch (absolute) or an elected parliament and prime minister (constitutional).
s: Hereditary succession named
No, with the test of who holds the power

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The head of state of the United Kingdom exercises the real power of the executive.
Reason (R): The United Kingdom has a king or queen as its head of state.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false: the king or queen has only nominal power and the prime minister exercises the real executive power. R is true, but a monarch as head of state does not mean the monarch holds executive power.

questions.q: Neha says, 'Iran's president is elected by the people, so the people also choose the person who holds the ultimate authority.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The elected president and parliament take care of everyday governance. The person with ultimate authority over the legislature, executive and judiciary is the Supreme Leader, who is selected by a group of Islamic clerics and holds the post for life.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The elected president and parliament handle everyday governance
The Supreme Leader holds ultimate authority and is selected by clerics for life

questions.q: Which set of facts is enough, by itself, to classify a country as an absolute monarchy?
o: The monarch makes laws, ensures they are followed, judges disputes and need not heed the council
The monarch inherits the throne and appoints a council of advisers to assist the government
The monarch is the head of state and opens the sessions of the legislature each year
The monarch follows the rules of a religion and the country has an elected parliament too
questions.a: Complete control over making, enforcing and adjudicating laws is the mark of an absolute monarchy, as in Saudi Arabia where the king is not bound by his council. Inheriting the throne is true of monarchs in general, and the other facts fit a constitutional monarchy or a mixed system.

questions.q: A king who is an absolute monarch wants to look more democratic. Plan A: appoint a council of 30 advisers. Plan B: hand law-making to an elected parliament and executive power to a prime minister. (a) Which plan changes the type of monarchy, and into what? (b) Why does the other plan leave the monarchy as it was?
questions.a: (a) Plan B, which makes it a constitutional monarchy: the king would have only nominal power. (b) An absolute monarch can appoint a council that advises him, as in Saudi Arabia, but he is not bound by its advice, so he still controls the laws.
s: (a) Plan B; constitutional monarchy
(b) A council that only advises leaves the monarch's control intact

questions.q:
Match each fictional land in Column A with the best description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Land P: the king writes the laws and appoints a 10-member council whose advice he may ignore.  2. Land Q: the queen opens the legislature; elected members pass the laws; a prime minister leads the Council of Ministers.  3. Land R: a leader chosen for life by clerics overrules the elected parliament.  4. Land S: the eldest son succeeded his father as monarch (nothing else is known).
Column B: a. Constitutional monarchy  b. Absolute monarchy  c. Theocracy  d. The type cannot be told from this fact alone
questions.a: P matches an absolute monarchy and Q a constitutional monarchy. R matches a theocracy, in which the ruling authority is a religious leader. S only tells us that monarchies are usually hereditary; the type depends on who holds the power.

questions.q: 'The name or title a country uses does not tell us how it is governed.' Justify with the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia and Iran.
questions.a: Both the UK and Saudi Arabia have a king or queen, yet the UK's has only nominal power and Saudi Arabia's holds all power. Iran's official name is the Islamic Republic of Iran and it has an elected president and parliament, yet the Supreme Leader, selected by clerics for life, has the ultimate authority over the legislature, executive and judiciary. So the real power must be read from how the government works.
s: UK: king or queen with only nominal power
Saudi Arabia: king with complete control
Iran: official name Islamic Republic and elected bodies, but the Supreme Leader holds ultimate authority
Draws the conclusion that real power must be read from the working of the government

questions.q: A student says, 'Iran must be a plain democracy, because it has an elected president and an elected parliament.' Which reply uses the chapter best?
o: They handle everyday governance, but the Supreme Leader chosen by clerics for life holds ultimate authority
They are the highest authority, since the Supreme Leader is selected by the president and works under the parliament
They show Iran is a democracy like India, since the chapter says elected bodies decide the form of a government
They show Iran is an absolute monarchy, since a leader chosen for life is the same as a hereditary king
questions.a: The chapter says Iran combines theocratic and democratic elements: an elected president and parliament manage everyday governance, but the Supreme Leader, selected by a group of Islamic clerics for life, has the ultimate authority over the legislature, executive and judiciary.

questions.q: A traveller writes, 'Britain has a king, so it is a monarchy and therefore cannot be a democracy.' (a) What part of this is right? (b) Which sentence of the chapter shows the conclusion is wrong, and why?
questions.a: (a) Britain does have a king or queen as head of state, so it is a monarchy. (b) The chapter says that while Britain has a king, it really is today a parliamentary democracy: the elected parliament makes the laws and the prime minister with the Council of Ministers exercises the executive power, while the monarch has only nominal power.
s: (a) Britain is a monarchy since it has a king or queen as head of state
(b) Parliament makes laws and the prime minister rules; the monarch is nominal, so it is also a parliamentary democracy

questions.q: Compare absolute monarchy, constitutional monarchy and theocracy on who holds real power and how that person comes to power. Then analyse which of the three is closest to a democracy.
questions.a: Absolute monarchy (Saudi Arabia): the king holds all power, inherited, and need not follow his council. Constitutional monarchy (UK): the monarch is nominal, the prime minister and elected parliament hold power. Theocracy (Iran): religion and leaders rule, with a Supreme Leader selected by clerics for life. The constitutional monarchy is closest to democracy because parliament is elected.
s: Absolute monarchy: real power and succession
Constitutional monarchy: real power and succession
Theocracy: real power and how the leader is selected
Names constitutional monarchy as closest to democracy
Reason: elected parliament and prime minister, with nominal monarch

questions.q: Taking Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and Iran as the chapter describes them, in which pair does the person at the top hold authority over making laws, carrying them out and judging disputes?
o: Saudi Arabia and Iran, through the king and the Supreme Leader in each
The United Kingdom and Iran, through the monarch and the Supreme Leader respectively
The United Kingdom and Saudi Arabia, through the monarch and the king respectively
Only Saudi Arabia, because Iran's Supreme Leader leaves law-making to the parliament
questions.a: In Saudi Arabia the king holds all power, and in Iran the Supreme Leader has the ultimate authority over the legislature, executive and judiciary. In the UK the king or queen has only nominal power.

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'The United Kingdom and Saudi Arabia are both monarchies, but they differ most in who makes the laws.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Both have a king or queen, but in Saudi Arabia, an absolute monarchy, the king has complete control in making the laws, whereas in the United Kingdom the laws are made by the elected parliament and the monarch has only nominal power.
s: Verdict: yes, both are monarchies
Saudi Arabia: the king controls law-making
UK: the elected parliament makes the laws

questions.q: In Iran an elected president and parliament take care of everyday governance. (a) Over which organs does the chapter say the Supreme Leader has ultimate authority? (b) What does this show about how far 'elected' goes in Iran's system?
questions.a: (a) The legislature, the executive and the judiciary. (b) The elected bodies work under the Supreme Leader's ultimate authority; being elected does not make them the final authority, so Iran is a mix of theocratic and democratic elements.
s: (a) Legislature, executive and judiciary
(b) Elected bodies handle everyday governance but are not the final authority

questions.q:
Three fictional lands. Land A: the king alone makes the laws, enforces them and judges disputes; his council of 20 only advises him. Land B: the queen is head of state, an elected parliament of 300 makes the laws and a prime minister with ministers exercises executive power. Land C: a Supreme Leader chosen for life by clerics has ultimate authority, and an elected president and parliament handle everyday governance. In Land C the elected parliament passes a law that the Supreme Leader opposes.
(a) Classify A, B and C as absolute monarchy, constitutional monarchy or theocracy.
(b) Whose view is likely to prevail in Land C, and what does this show about the limit of 'elected' there?
(c) The king of A offers to ask his 20 councillors about every law. Does this change A's type? Why?
(d) In which land do the people have the most say in making the laws? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) A absolute monarchy, B constitutional monarchy, C theocracy. (b) The Supreme Leader's, because he has the ultimate authority over the legislature, executive and judiciary; the elected parliament works under that authority. (c) No: he need not follow their advice, so he still controls the laws. (d) Land B, where an elected parliament makes the laws.
s: Part (a): all three classified correctly
Part (b): the Supreme Leader prevails; elected bodies are not the final authority
Part (c): no change, since the council only advises and the king is not bound
Part (d): Land B, with the elected parliament as the reason

questions.q:
In Country M, the king opens each session of parliament and greets visitors, while the elected parliament makes all the laws. Recently a group of citizens submitted a petition: 'The king should be given the power to cancel any law, to protect the people from hasty decisions.' Some argue this is wise; others fear a return to times when kings held all power.
(a) Which type of monarchy is Country M, and on what evidence?
(b) Who exercises executive power in such a country?
(c) If the petition is accepted, which function of government would the king begin to control, and towards which type of monarchy would M move?
(d) Decide whether the petition should be accepted, giving one point in its favour and one against.
questions.a: (a) Constitutional monarchy: the monarch has nominal duties while the elected parliament makes laws. (b) The prime minister with the Council of Ministers. (c) The legislative function, moving towards an absolute monarchy (a trend, not yet a change of type). (d) A reasoned decision, for example rejecting it: a veto can protect against hasty laws but it gives a hereditary ruler control of law-making, as in Saudi Arabia.
s: Part (a): constitutional monarchy, with parliament making the laws as evidence
Part (b): prime minister and council of ministers
Part (c): the legislative function; towards absolute monarchy
Part (d): a decision with a point for and a point against
