questions.q: Dev says, 'A small group can hold absolute power in a dictatorship, and that makes a dictatorship exactly the same thing as an oligarchy.' Is he right? Use the chapter's descriptions.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter's definition of a dictatorship says one person or a small group possesses absolute power with no limits from a constitution or law, so a small group can be a dictatorship. But an oligarchy is described as a small, powerful group, usually wealthy families or influential people, making the important decisions; the two are separate types, not exactly the same.
s: Right part: a small group can hold absolute power
Wrong part: the two types are defined differently
Verdict partly right

questions.q: In the chapter's account of Adolf Hitler, which step made him a dictator?
o: Passing laws that gave him full power and removed the opposition
Being appointed Chancellor of Germany by the leaders of his country
Believing that his own people were superior to all other peoples
Starting a war in 1939 that spread to many countries around the world
questions.a: The chapter says that soon after he was appointed Chancellor in 1933 he passed laws that gave him full power and eliminated the opposition; he was now a dictator. His appointment, beliefs and the war come before or after that step.

questions.q: Classify each as a dictatorship, an oligarchy or both, using the chapter's descriptions: (i) a general who bans all parties and rules by decree; (ii) five wealthy families who control the decisions of an elected council; (iii) a committee of three officers who rule without any limit from a constitution or law.
questions.a: (i) Dictatorship: one person holds absolute power with no limit. (ii) Oligarchy: a small powerful group of wealthy families makes the important decisions, though the council is elected. (iii) Both: a small group with absolute power is a dictatorship, and a small powerful group making the decisions is an oligarchy.
s: (i) Dictatorship, with the reason
(ii) Oligarchy, with the reason
(iii) Both, with the reason

questions.q: A student argues, 'A ruler who faces no limits can get things done faster, so a dictatorship is better for ordinary people than a slow democracy.' Evaluate this claim using Hitler, Idi Amin and Shane's story.
questions.a: A dictatorship is absolute power with no limit from a constitution or law, so speed is possible. But Hitler's unlimited power led to the killing of at least six million Jews and hundreds of thousands of Roma, and to World War II (1939-1945). Idi Amin killed thousands and forced many Indians to flee. In Shane's story the government decides hair and clothes, blocks the global internet and has people report on one another. Because nothing limits the ruler, nothing stops harm to people, so speed does not make ordinary people better off.
s: Explains why unlimited power can act quickly
Hitler: the Holocaust and World War II
Idi Amin: killings and Indians forced to flee
Shane: loss of choice and information
Concludes that without limits nothing stops harm, so the claim fails

questions.q: General X rules the country within a constitution that courts enforce on him. General Y rules by decrees that no constitution or court can limit. Which statement agrees with the chapter?
o: Y is the dictator, because absolute power with no legal limit is the mark, not being a soldier
X is the dictator, because any general who runs a government is always a dictator
Both are dictators, because both are generals who rule over many civilians
Neither is a dictator, because a dictator must be elected by a free vote of all adults
questions.a: A dictatorship is a government in which one person or a small group possesses absolute power with no limits imposed by a constitution or law. Y matches; X is limited by a constitution and courts.

questions.q:
Read the statements about dictatorship and oligarchy.
1. Adolf Hitler became a dictator on the day he was appointed Chancellor of Germany.
2. A body whose members are all elected can still show signs of oligarchy if a small group holds too much influence.
3. In a dictatorship, the holder of absolute power may be one person or a small group.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: he became a dictator after the appointment, by passing laws giving himself full power. Statements 2 and 3 are the chapter's descriptions of oligarchy in democracies and of dictatorship.

questions.q: (a) Adolf Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany. Was the appointment itself what made him a dictator? Explain. (b) Give the year of his appointment and the years of World War II as the chapter gives them, and find how many years after his appointment the war began.
questions.a: (a) No. He became a dictator after the appointment, when he passed laws that gave him full power and eliminated the opposition. (b) Appointed 1933; the war ran 1939-1945; it began 1939 - 1933 = 6 years after his appointment.
s: Dictator because of what he did after appointment

questions.q: True or False: Hitler and Idi Amin are examples of oligarchy, because each ruled on behalf of a small group of wealthy families. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter presents Hitler and Idi Amin as dictators, each a single ruler with absolute power. An oligarchy is rule by a small, powerful group, usually wealthy families or influential people.
s: Verdict False
Reason: they were dictators, one person with absolute power, not a ruling group of wealthy families

questions.q: Two refugees tell their stories. Meena's family, descended from Indians who had settled in Uganda a few generations earlier, was forced to flee. Tobias's family lost relatives in a campaign that killed at least six million Jews. Which pairing agrees with the chapter?
o: Meena: Idi Amin; Tobias: Adolf Hitler
Meena: Adolf Hitler; Tobias: Idi Amin
Meena and Tobias: both Adolf Hitler
Meena and Tobias: both Idi Amin
questions.a: Idi Amin was the military dictator of Uganda who forced many Indians to flee; Adolf Hitler was responsible for the killing of at least six million Jews.

questions.q: Elections are held in Town T, but three wealthy families fund every candidate and nothing passes the council without their approval. By the chapter's term, T shows signs of ___ (one word).
questions.a: oligarchy

questions.q: Can a democracy slowly turn into an oligarchy? Explain how this could happen, and give two things people can do to keep democracy strong.
questions.a: Oligarchy is rule by a small powerful group, often wealthy families. A democracy can show signs of it when a small group of politicians and wealthy businesspeople hold too much influence even though members are elected. People can stay vigilant and vote, changing representatives through elections, and keep the judiciary independent and information channels free.
s: Defines oligarchy
How it can happen: too much influence of a few over an elected system
First action by people
Second action by people

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Hitler became a dictator only after the laws he passed in 1933.
Reason (R): The laws he passed gave him full power and eliminated the opposition.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: he was appointed Chancellor, and it was the laws giving him full power and removing the opposition that made him a dictator.

questions.q: Compare oligarchy in ancient Greece with the signs of oligarchy the chapter sees in some democracies today. (a) Who formed the ruling group in each? (b) What does the cartoon of an elected body in the USA in the late 19th century, in which all those shown were elected, show about how a small group can rule?
questions.a: (a) Ancient Greece: aristocratic families; today: a small group of politicians and wealthy businesspeople who hold too much influence. (b) Even in a body whose members are all elected, a few of them can make the important decisions, so being elected does not by itself prevent rule by a few.
s: (a) Aristocratic families and politicians with wealthy businesspeople
(b) Elected members, yet a few decide: election alone does not prevent oligarchy

questions.q: Shane says, 'We all want to explore new styles, but the government decides the way we should keep our hair.' Which principle of democracy from the chapter's list does this contradict?
o: Freedom, the right to make one's own choices and to express opinions freely
Representative participation, the right to elect one's representatives
Independent judiciary, which makes all parts of the government follow the law
Universal adult franchise, the right of every adult citizen to vote
questions.a: Freedom in a democracy means that citizens have the right to make their own choices and express their opinions. A government deciding every citizen's haircut takes that away.

questions.q: Write three rules that a dictatorship might impose on students in a school, and name the principle of democracy each one breaks.
questions.a: Examples: only one hair style is allowed (freedom); students must report classmates who break rules (freedom and equality); only the grade 12 may ever vote (universal adult franchise or equality). Each rule is paired with a correct principle.
s: First rule with a matching principle
Second rule with a matching principle
Third rule with a matching principle

questions.q: Shane tells the tourist that the government decides the way everyone cuts their hair. (a) Which principle of democracy does this break? (b) What, according to the chapter, would a person in a democracy be free to do about hair and clothes, and where does that freedom stop?
questions.a: (a) Freedom. (b) In a democracy people can choose what to wear and how to express themselves, until and unless it harms someone else's rights.
s: (a) Freedom
(b) Free to choose what to wear until it harms someone else's rights

questions.q: A commentator says, 'A council whose members were all elected can never be an oligarchy.' Which new fact would show the commentator is wrong?
o: Five of nine elected members, all from wealthy families, settle nearly all decisions in private
The council's nine members were elected for a term of five years each, as the law requires
The council meets once a month and publishes its final budget every single year
The council has a larger yearly budget than the council of the neighbouring town
questions.a: The chapter notes that even some democracies show signs of oligarchy when a small group of politicians and wealthy businesspeople hold too much influence in governance. The other facts say nothing about a small group making the decisions.

questions.q: (a) Which groups of people did the chapter say suffered under Hitler and under Idi Amin respectively? (b) What does it suggest about a ruler with no limit from a constitution or law that such groups could be targeted?
questions.a: (a) Under Hitler, Jews (at least six million killed), hundreds of thousands of Roma and others; under Amin, thousands killed and many Indians forced to flee. (b) With no constitution or law limiting them, such rulers could target groups without being stopped.
s: (a) Jews, Roma and others under Hitler; Indians (and thousands killed) under Amin
(b) No legal limit meant nothing could stop the targeting

questions.q:
Kolara is ruled by Ruler R, who came to power after the army removed the elected government. His decrees cannot be questioned by any constitution or court, newspapers that criticise him are shut, and opposition leaders have been jailed. Anyone who votes against him at a public meeting is sent away from the town. He has, however, built free hospitals in every district.
(a) Which type of government does Kolara most resemble, and which features from the chapter's definition match?
(b) Name two principles of democracy that Ruler R is breaking.
(c) Citizens of a democracy can change a failing government by voting. What can the people of Kolara do instead, and what does that show?
(d) A visitor says, 'With free hospitals in every district, Kolara's people are better off than under a slow democracy.' Give one point for and one against, and decide.
questions.a: (a) A dictatorship: one person rules with no limit from a constitution or law, and opposition is removed. (b) Any two of: freedom (of speech/press), universal adult franchise or representative participation, independent judiciary, fundamental rights, equality. (c) They cannot remove him by voting; the people have no say, unlike in a democracy. (d) For: the hospitals meet a real need. Against: with no limits on the ruler, no freedom, no independent court and no vote, the people cannot hold him to account, as in Shane's story. Any decision that weighs the hospitals against the missing limits and rights is accepted.
s: Part (a): dictatorship, with matching features
Part (b): two principles named correctly
Part (c): no way to change the ruler by voting, tied to the people's lack of say
Part (d): one point for, one against and a decision

questions.q:
Nirmalpur's town council has nine elected members. Five of them come from three wealthy families who own the textile mills. Last year the council took 40 decisions: 34 were settled in private meetings of these five, and only 6 were openly debated. A citizens' group offers two plans: Plan 1, a rule that every decision must be debated openly and recorded; Plan 2, putting up its own candidates at the next election.
(a) What does it say about the council that 34 of the 40 decisions were settled privately by five members?
(b) Which type of government does the council show signs of, and how does the root of the word describe it?
(c) Why is it possible for this to happen although all nine members were elected?
(d) Which plan would you support, or would you combine them? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 85% of decisions were taken by a few, which shows control by a small group. (b) Oligarchy: oligos means few and arkho means to rule. (c) Elections do not prevent a small group of wealthy people from holding too much influence over decisions. (d) A reasoned choice: Plan 1 gives immediate transparency; Plan 2 uses the elections, by which people can change their representatives; supporting both is also defensible.
s: Part (a): most decisions (34 of 40) taken by a few, showing control by a small group
Part (b): oligarchy, rule by a few
Part (c): a few wealthy people can hold too much influence over elected members
Part (d): a reasoned choice using the chapter's idea of elections and vigilance

questions.q: Which of these claims of 'freedom' would NOT be protected, using the chapter's test of when freedom ends?
o: A factory owner dumps waste in a village well, calling it his freedom to run the factory
A student chooses to wear a cap of her own choice and says so openly in the school assembly
A citizen criticises a government decision in a speech held in the open town square
A family follows its own beliefs at home and does not ask others to follow the same beliefs
questions.a: The chapter says people can live as they want in a democracy until and unless it harms someone else's rights. Poisoning a well harms the villagers' rights; the other three are choices that harm nobody.

questions.q: Aman fills the oligarchy column of the chapter's Table 9.2 with 'Yes' for universal adult franchise. Which reasoning shows his mistake?
o: An oligarchy is rule by a few, so not every adult has the vote
Only an absolute monarchy lets every adult vote, never an oligarchy
An oligarchy has an independent judiciary, which removes the vote
The wealthy families in an oligarchy are elected by the adults
questions.a: Table 9.2 marks No for oligarchy because the word means rule by a few; power sits with a small group, not with every adult voting. The other options give reasons the chapter does not make.

questions.q:
Read the statements about why democracy matters.
1. One reason the chapter gives for most countries considering democracy better is that the people choose their government.
2. Since more than half of the world's countries are democracies, every democracy is free of the hurdles the chapter lists.
3. Wealth disparity and manipulation of information channels are among the hurdles the chapter lists for democracy.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says even democracies have problems, however many countries have adopted democracy.

questions.q: (a) Does the fact that more than half of the world's countries have adopted democracy by itself prove democracy is better? (b) Give two reasons from the chapter why most countries consider it a better form.
questions.a: (a) No: popularity alone proves nothing; the reasons must come from how it works. (b) Any two of: the people choose their government; the government is accountable for rights and basic needs; people can change representatives through elections; people have freedom of choice.
s: Popularity is not proof, with reason
Two reasons

questions.q: A survey of 40 countries matches the chapter's statement about how many of the world's countries have adopted democracy, using the smallest whole number that fits. The sample has ___ democracies.

Match each situation in Column A with the hurdle to democracy it shows in Column B.
Column A: 1. Newspapers print only what a few powerful people allow.  2. Judges are moved to distant courts when they rule against ministers.  3. Ten families fund every party and settle the council's decisions.  4. Officials take money to clear files.
Column B: a. Manipulation of information channels  b. Erosion of the judiciary's independence  c. Excessive control by a few over democratic institutions  d. Corruption
questions.a: Controlling what is printed is manipulation of information channels; moving judges for their rulings erodes the judiciary's independence; ten families settling decisions is control by a few; bribes are corruption.

questions.q: Explain the phrase 'excessive control by a few over democratic institutions' with an example from a school student council.
questions.a: It means a small group has too much power over bodies like parliament or courts. For example, three students decide everything for a council of fifteen and the elected representatives of other classes are ignored.
s: Explains the phrase: a small group holds too much influence over the institutions
A suitable example of a few dominating a council

questions.q: Which pair correctly names a hurdle from the chapter and what it puts at risk?
o: Erosion of the judiciary's independence: protection of citizens' fundamental rights
Corruption: the holding of elections at all, since corrupt officials cannot allow any votes
Wealth disparity: the independence of the judiciary, which then becomes automatic everywhere
Manipulation of information channels: the right of adults to vote, which is then lost entirely
questions.a: An independent judiciary ensures that fundamental rights are protected and that all parts of the government follow the laws, so eroding its independence puts that protection at risk. The other pairings link a hurdle to something the chapter does not connect it with.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A democratic government can be changed by the voters if it performs poorly.
Reason (R): In a democracy the people may choose what to speak, wear and believe, until and unless it harms someone else's rights.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true: if the government does not perform its functions properly, people can change their representatives through elections. R describes the freedom of citizens, a different feature, so it does not explain A.

questions.q: True or False: A democracy can face problems such as corruption and wealth disparity and yet still be considered better than other forms of government by most countries. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter admits that even democracies have problems, but they allow people to choose their government and to change their representatives through elections, which is a constant check on the government.
s: Verdict True
Reason: the elections check even with problems

questions.q: In a democracy the judiciary's independence is slowly being eroded. (a) Which of the hurdles listed in the chapter is this? (b) Using the chapter's earlier principle of an independent judiciary, say what citizens would lose.
questions.a: (a) Erosion of the judiciary's independence. (b) An independent judiciary ensures that every citizen's fundamental rights are protected and that laws are followed by citizens and by all parts of the government; without it these protections weaken.
s: (a) Erosion of the judiciary's independence
(b) Protection of fundamental rights and obedience to the law by the government itself

questions.q: Kabir says, 'In a democracy people can choose what to speak, wear and believe, and nobody can ever limit this, because it is the rule of the people.' Is he right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. People can indeed choose what to speak, wear and believe in a democracy, but only until and unless it harms someone else's rights, so the freedom does have a limit.
s: Right part: the freedoms exist
Wrong part: limit when it harms others' rights
Verdict partly right

questions.q: In a democracy, a newspaper stops printing stories about corruption after a few businesspeople pressurise its editor, and judges who rule against ministers are moved to other courts. What does the chapter ask citizens to do?
o: Remain vigilant, as individuals and as a society, to keep such hurdles small
Accept it, since a democracy with these problems has already stopped being a democracy
Give up elections and hand decisions to a ruler who is not limited by any law
Leave it to ministers and judges, since citizens have no part in a democracy
questions.a: The chapter lists manipulation of information channels and erosion of the judiciary's independence as hurdles and asks what individuals and society can do to remain vigilant and minimise them. It does not say democracy is lost, nor that citizens have no part.

questions.q: A town spends 90% of its yearly budget on a road to the mayor's own village. (a) Which ideal that the chapter says should guide a democratic government is being ignored? (b) What can the town's people do about it, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) The well-being of all its people. (b) They can change their representatives through elections, which is a constant check on the government, and remain vigilant.
s: (a) Well-being of all its people
(b) Change representatives through elections and stay vigilant

questions.q: Show that a government that cancels elections for ten years cannot be accountable to its people in the sense the chapter gives.
questions.a: Accountable means answerable to the people who elected it. The chapter says that if a government fails, people change their representatives through elections. Without elections the people have no way to do this, so the government is not answerable to them.
s: States the meaning of accountability: answerable to the people who elected it
States that elections are the way to change representatives
Concludes that without elections there is no answerability

questions.q: A minister says, 'We hold elections every five years, so excessive control of our institutions by a few can never arise here.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: Elections do not rule it out: the chapter lists control by a few over democratic institutions as a hurdle
The minister is right, because the chapter says that elected governments are always free of all hurdles
The minister is right, because control by a few is a problem only of absolute monarchies and kingdoms
The minister is wrong, because a country that holds elections every five years is not a democracy at all
questions.a: The chapter says that even democracies have problems, and names excessive control by a few over democratic institutions among them. Holding elections is a feature of democracy but does not guarantee the hurdles are absent.

questions.q: Write a short situation (three or four lines) in which the people of a town use elections to correct a failing government. Show clearly what was wrong and what changed.
questions.a: A good situation shows a government failing in a function such as providing water or protecting rights, then the people electing new representatives, and the change acting as a check on the government.
s: Shows a failure of the government's functions
Shows the people using an election to change representatives
Shows the outcome as a check on the government

questions.q: Compare democracy and dictatorship on (a) universal adult franchise, (b) what people may speak and wear, (c) what happens when the government fails, and (d) the goals of the government. Then say why most countries prefer democracy.
questions.a: Franchise: democracy yes, dictatorship no. Freedoms: democracy allows choices unless they harm others' rights; in a dictatorship the government decides, as in Shane's story. Failure: democracy changes representatives by election; a dictator has no such check. Goals: a democracy aims at the well-being of all people, while a dictatorship pursues the aims the ruler sets, with no say for the people, as in Shane's story. questions.q:
Three countries are described. Country P: every adult can vote, the media are free and the courts are independent. Country Q: rulers come only from three families, no election has been held for 40 years, and newspapers print only what the government approves. Country R: elections are held every five years, but ten wealthy families fund every party and officials pressurise the courts.
(a) Which country is a democracy working well, and which shows signs of democracy in trouble?
(b) Name two challenges to democracy that Country R shows.
(c) Which of P and Q lets the people remove a failing government by voting, and how can you tell?
(d) A citizen of R says, 'Voting is pointless now: the ten families win whoever we choose.' Her neighbour says, 'If we stop voting, the one check we still have is gone.' Weigh the two views and advise her.
questions.a: (a) P works well; R is a democracy in trouble. (b) Excessive control by a few over democratic institutions (wealthy families funding every party), and erosion of the judiciary's independence (pressure on courts). (c) P: every adult can vote, so a failing government can be voted out; Q cannot, as no election has been held for 40 years. (d) The first view has force since the wealthy families dominate the parties; the neighbour's view is that elections are the people's way to change representatives and must be used along with vigilance. Any advice that weighs both is accepted.
s: Part (a): P democracy working well; R democracy in trouble
Part (b): control by a few and pressure on the courts named
Part (c): P can remove its government by voting, Q cannot
Part (d): weighs the frustration against the value of the election check and advises

questions.q:
The Student Council of Vidya Vihar School has 15 members, one elected from each class, and an annual fund of ₹3,60,000. The accounts show: 40% spent on the library, 25% on sports, and the remaining 35% spent on events organised by only two members for their own friends. Students are upset.
(a) How much was spent on the events for the two members' friends?
(b) Which feature of democracy lets the students act, and how?
(c) Which challenge to democracy from the chapter does this resemble?
(d) Two plans are offered. Plan 1: the Council must publish its accounts and every large spending needs the approval of the class representatives. Plan 2: wait and vote the two members out at the next annual election. Which should the school choose, or should it combine them? Justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 35% of 3,60,000 = ₹1,26,000. (b) Elections: students can change their representatives by voting them out. (c) Corruption, or excessive control by a few. (d) A reasoned choice: Plan 1 checks the misuse now but needs the vigilance of the representatives; Plan 2 uses the election check but allows a year of misuse. Combining both is defensible.
s: Part (b): elections let people change their representatives
Part (c): corruption or control by a few
Part (d): a decision weighing the two plans using the chapter's ideas of elections and vigilance
